questions.question: The principal focus of a concave mirror is the point where:

options.text: Rays parallel to the principal axis appear to diverge after reflection
The mirror surface intersects the principal axis
Rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflection
Rays passing through the center of curvature converge

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflection**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **concave mirror** is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved **inwards**, facing towards the center of the sphere. It is also known as a **converging mirror** because it converges the light rays incident on it.
 
• The **Principal Focus (F)** of a concave mirror is a specific point on its **principal axis**. When rays of light coming from infinity or a distant source are **parallel** to the principal axis, they strike the mirror and, after reflection, actually **meet or converge** at this point. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• Unlike a convex mirror, the focus of a concave mirror is a **real focus** because the light rays actually pass through it. It is situated in **front** of the reflecting surface.
 
• The distance from the **pole (P)** of the mirror to the **principal focus (F)** is called the **focal length (f)** of the mirror.
 
• The **principal axis** is the straight line passing through the **pole** and the **center of curvature** of the spherical mirror.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components of Spherical Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Pole (P):** The **center** of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror. The intersection of the mirror surface and the principal axis defines this point. ***Hence, statement 2 describes the pole and is incorrect.***
 
• **Center of Curvature (C):** The center of the **hollow sphere** of which the mirror is a part. For a concave mirror, it lies in front of it, while for a convex mirror, it lies behind it.
 
• **Radius of Curvature (R):** The distance between the **pole** and the **center of curvature**.
 
 
 
• **Rules of Reflection:**
 
 
• A ray passing through the **center of curvature** of a concave mirror is reflected back along the **same path** because it hits the mirror at an **angle of incidence of 0 degrees** (perpendicular to the surface). It does not converge at the focus upon reflection from C. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• In a **convex mirror**, rays parallel to the principal axis **diverge** after reflection and only **appear** to originate from the focus located behind the mirror. ***Hence, statement 1 describes a convex mirror and is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Image Formation:** Concave mirrors can form both **real** and **virtual** images, as well as **magnified** or **diminished** images, depending on the position of the object relative to the **focus** and **center of curvature**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mathematical Relation:** For spherical mirrors with small apertures, the **radius of curvature (R)** is exactly **twice** the **focal length (f)**, represented by the formula **R = 2f**.
 
• **Uses of Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• They are commonly used in **torches**, **search-lights**, and **vehicle headlights** to get powerful parallel beams of light.
 
• They are used as **shaving mirrors** to see a larger image of the face.
 
• **Dentists** use concave mirrors to see **enlarged images** of the teeth of patients.
 
• Large concave mirrors are used to **concentrate sunlight** to produce heat in **solar furnaces**.
 
 
 
• **Sign Convention:** According to the **New Cartesian Sign Convention**, the focal length of a **concave mirror** is always taken as **negative**, whereas for a **convex mirror**, it is **positive**.
</ul

questions.question: What does a blue, non-luminous flame indicate when a hydrocarbon is burnt?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Complete combustion with high temperature**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **blue, non-luminous flame** is the characteristic result of **complete combustion** of a hydrocarbon. This occurs when the fuel reacts with a **sufficient supply of oxygen**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• In **complete combustion**, the hydrocarbon is fully oxidized, producing only **carbon dioxide (CO2)** and **water vapor (H2O)** as chemical byproducts, along with a significant release of **heat and light energy**.
 
• The **blue color** of the flame is primarily due to the emission from **excited molecular fragments** like **CH and C2 radicals**. Because there are no **unburnt carbon particles** (soot) present to glow, the flame does not appear yellow or luminous. 
 
• This type of flame indicates a **high temperature**, often reaching between **1400°C and 1650°C** in a standard Bunsen burner setup. This efficiency makes it ideal for **industrial heating** and laboratory experiments.
 
• Conversely, a **yellow flame** indicates **incomplete combustion**, which happens when **oxygen is limited**. This results in the formation of **soot** and **carbon monoxide**. ***Hence, statements 2, 3, and 4 are incorrect descriptions of a blue flame.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Luminous vs. Non-Luminous Flames**:
 
 
• **Luminous Flame**: These are typically **yellow-orange** and occur during **incomplete combustion**. The luminosity is caused by **incandescence**, where tiny particles of **unburnt carbon** (soot) are heated to a point where they emit visible light.
 
• **Non-Luminous Flame**: These are **blue** and occur during **complete combustion**. They do not produce smoke or soot, making them "cleaner" for the environment and equipment.
 
 
 
• **Hydrocarbons**: These are organic compounds consisting entirely of **hydrogen and carbon**. Common examples include **Methane (CH4)**, **Propane (C3H8)**, and **Butane (C4H10)**. **Saturated hydrocarbons** (alkanes) generally burn with a blue flame if oxygen is plenty, while **unsaturated hydrocarbons** (alkenes/alkynes) often burn with a sooty flame due to higher carbon percentages.
 
• **The Bunsen Burner**: Developed by **Robert Bunsen** in **1855**, this device allows for the adjustment of the **air-to-gas ratio**. By opening the **air hole**, more oxygen mixes with the gas, producing a **roaring blue flame** used for high-heat applications.
 
• **Chemical Equation**: The general equation for the complete combustion of **Methane** is: **CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + Heat Energy**. If oxygen is insufficient, the reaction might produce **Carbon Monoxide (CO)** or **Solid Carbon (C)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Soot Formation**: **Soot** consists of fine **black carbon particles**. It is a major pollutant and can cause respiratory issues. Its presence in a flame is a clear indicator that the fuel is not being utilized **efficiently**.
 
• **Oxygen Supply**: The **oxygen-to-fuel ratio** is the most critical factor determining flame type. In household **LPG stoves**, the burners are designed with small holes to ensure a steady supply of air, which is why they normally produce a **blue flame**. If the flame turns yellow, it usually indicates the **air holes are blocked**.
 
• **Temperature Zones**: In a flame, the **outermost zone** (non-luminous) is the **hottest part** because it has direct access to atmospheric oxygen. The **middle zone** (luminous) is moderately hot, and the **innermost zone** (containing unburnt vapors) is the **coolest**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between mass and inertia?

options.text: Mass is inversely proportional to inertia
Mass is directly proportional to the square of inertia
Mass is directly proportional to inertia

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mass is directly proportional to inertia**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Inertia** is defined as the inherent property of a physical object to resist any change in its state of **rest** or **uniform motion** in a straight line. 
• The **mass** of an object is a quantitative measure of its **inertia**. It represents the amount of matter contained within an object and determines how much it will resist acceleration when a **force** is applied. 
• There is a **linear and direct relationship** between these two concepts. A body with a **heavier mass** possesses **greater inertia**, meaning it is harder to start moving if it is at rest, or harder to stop if it is already moving. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.*** 
• According to **Newton's First Law of Motion**, also known as the **Law of Inertia**, an object will maintain its state of motion unless an external **unbalanced force** acts upon it. 
• Because **inertia** depends solely on the **mass** of the object, any increase in mass results in a corresponding and proportional increase in the object's resistance to changes in motion. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Types of Inertia:** 
• **Inertia of Rest:** The inability of a body to change its state of rest by itself. For example, when a **bus** starts suddenly, the passengers tend to fall backward because their lower body moves with the bus while the upper body tries to remain at **rest**. 
• **Inertia of Motion:** The inability of a body to change its state of uniform motion by itself. For example, an **athlete** runs some distance before taking a long jump to gain momentum and overcome the tendency to stop. 
• **Inertia of Direction:** The inability of a body to change its **direction of motion** by itself. For instance, when a car rounds a curve sharply, the passengers are thrown toward the outside of the curve. 
• **Newton's Second Law Connection:** 
• The relationship is further clarified by **Newton's Second Law** (**F = ma**). Here, **mass (m)** acts as the proportionality constant between **force (F)** and **acceleration (a)**. For a constant force, the larger the **mass**, the smaller the **acceleration**, illustrating the resistance provided by **inertia**. 
• **SI Units and Measurement:** 
• In the **International System of Units (SI)**, **mass** is measured in **kilograms (kg)**. **Inertia** does not have a separate unit of measurement; it is represented numerically by the object's **mass** value. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Analysis of Incorrect Statements:** 
• **Mass is independent of inertia:** This is incorrect because **mass** is fundamentally the measure of **inertia**. Without mass, there is no inertia in classical mechanics. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*** 
• **Mass is inversely proportional to inertia:** This statement implies that as an object gets heavier, it becomes easier to move, which contradicts the fundamental laws of **physics**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*** 
• **Mass is directly proportional to the square of inertia:** There is no quadratic relationship ($m \propto I²$) in the definition of these terms; the relationship is strictly **linear**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*** 
• **Historical Context:** 
• The concept of **Inertia** was first formulated by **Galileo Galilei** for horizontal motion on Earth and was later generalized by **Isaac Newton** in **1687** in his work "**Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica**".

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding 'changes of state of matter'?

A) A change of state of matter is a physical change.
B) A change of state of matter is an irreversible change.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only A**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Physical Change Definition:** A **physical change** is a type of change in which the **physical properties** of a substance, such as its **shape**, **size**, **color**, or **state**, undergo a transformation without altering its **chemical composition**. No new chemical substance is formed during this process.
 
• **Statement A Analysis:** When matter changes from one state to another (e.g., **liquid water** turning into **water vapor**), the **molecular structure** ($H_2O$) remains the same. Only the **kinetic energy** and the **arrangement of molecules** change. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• **Statement B Analysis:** A change of state is typically a **reversible change**. This means the substance can return to its original state by reversing the **external conditions** such as **temperature** or **pressure**. For instance, **ice** can melt into **water**, and that water can be **frozen** back into ice. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Conclusion:** Since only the first statement accurately describes the scientific nature of phase transitions, the final answer must reflect the validity of statement A alone. ***Hence, the correct answer is Only A.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **States of Matter:**
 
 
• Matter primarily exists in three states: **Solid**, **Liquid**, and **Gas**. Advanced states include **Plasma** and **Bose-Einstein Condensate**.
 
• **Solids** have a **definite shape** and **volume** due to strong **intermolecular forces**.
 
• **Liquids** have a **definite volume** but take the shape of the **container**.
 
• **Gases** have neither a **definite shape** nor a **definite volume**, filling all available space.
 
 
 
• **Processes of Phase Transition:**
 
 
• **Melting (Fusion):** The transition from a **solid** to a **liquid** state upon heating.
 
• **Freezing (Solidification):** The transition from a **liquid** to a **solid** state upon cooling.
 
• **Vaporization (Boiling/Evaporation):** The process where a **liquid** changes into a **gas**.
 
• **Condensation:** The process where a **gas** or vapor changes back into a **liquid**.
 
• **Sublimation:** A direct change from a **solid** to a **gas** without passing through the liquid phase (e.g., **Camphor** or **Dry Ice**).
 
• **Deposition:** A direct change from a **gas** to a **solid**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Energy:**
 
 
• Changes of state are driven by the **absorption** or **release** of **heat energy** (often referred to as **Latent Heat**).
 
• **Latent Heat of Fusion** is the heat required to change a substance from solid to liquid at its **melting point**.
 
• **Latent Heat of Vaporization** is the energy needed to convert a liquid into a gas at its **boiling point**.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Reversibility vs. Irreversibility:** While **physical changes** (like melting) are usually **reversible**, **chemical changes** (like burning wood or rusting iron) are typically **irreversible** because they result in the formation of new products with different properties.
 
• **Effect of Pressure:** While **temperature** is the most common factor, **pressure** also plays a critical role. For example, increasing pressure can **liquefy** certain gases (like **LPG** - Liquefied Petroleum Gas).
 
• **Constant Temperature:** During a change of state, the **temperature** of the substance remains **constant** even though heat is being supplied, as the energy is used to overcome **molecular attractions**.
</ul

questions.question: Unsaturated hydrocarbons usually produce:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**yellow flame with black smoke**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Unsaturated hydrocarbons** are organic compounds that contain at least one **double bond** (alkenes) or **triple bond** (alkynes) between carbon atoms.
 
• When **unsaturated hydrocarbons** are burnt in the presence of air, they typically undergo **incomplete combustion**. This happens because the proportion of **carbon** in these molecules is relatively high compared to **saturated hydrocarbons**.
 
• The high **carbon content** prevents all the carbon atoms from being completely oxidized into **carbon dioxide** given the limited amount of **oxygen** available in the surrounding air.
 
• As a result of this **incomplete combustion**, unburnt **carbon particles** are produced. These particles heat up and glow, giving the flame a characteristic **yellow color**.
 
• The unburnt carbon particles that do not glow or are released from the flame manifest as **soot** or **black smoke**. ***Hence, the statement that they produce a yellow flame with black smoke is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Saturated Hydrocarbons (Alkanes):** 
 
 
• Unlike unsaturated ones, **saturated hydrocarbons** like methane or ethane generally burn with a **clean blue flame** in sufficient air.
 
• This is because they have a lower **carbon-to-hydrogen ratio**, allowing for **complete combustion** where carbon is fully converted to **CO2**.
 
 
 
• **The Role of Oxygen:**
 
 
• The nature of the flame depends heavily on the **oxygen supply**. If an unsaturated hydrocarbon (like **acetylene**) is burnt in **pure oxygen** rather than air, it can undergo **complete combustion** and produce an extremely hot **blue flame** used in welding.
 
• In a **Bunsen burner**, closing the air holes leads to **incomplete combustion** and a **sooty yellow flame**, regardless of the fuel type.
 
 
 
• **Incandescence:**
 
 
• The **yellow light** emitted by the flame is a result of **incandescence**, which is the emission of light by a solid (the unburnt carbon) caused by its high **temperature**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Alkenes:** These are hydrocarbons with at least one **C=C double bond**. A common example is **Ethene** (C2H4).
 
• **Alkynes:** These contain at least one **C≡C triple bond**. A common example is **Ethyne** (C2H2), also known as **acetylene**.
 
• **Soot (Carbon Black):** The **black smoke** produced is essentially fine particles of **amorphous carbon**. It is industrially significant and used in the manufacturing of **tires** and **printing inks**.
 
• **Chemical Test:** Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons can be distinguished using the **Bromine Water Test**. Unsaturated hydrocarbons **decolorize** bromine water, whereas saturated ones do not react under normal conditions.

questions.question: Which metal is placed highest in the reactivity series?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sodium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **reactivity series** (or activity series) is a list of metals arranged in the **order of their decreasing chemical reactivity**. Metals at the top are most reactive, while those at the bottom are least reactive.
 
• Among the options provided, **Sodium** is the most reactive metal. In the standard reactivity series, **Potassium** sits at the very top, followed immediately by **Sodium**. ***Hence, the option Sodium is the correct answer.***
 
• **Sodium** (symbol **Na**, atomic number **11**) is an **alkali metal**. It reacts vigorously with both **oxygen** and **water** at room temperature, which is why it is never found in a free state in nature.
 
• **Copper** (symbol **Cu**), **Silver** (symbol **Ag**), and **Gold** (symbol **Au**) are placed much lower in the series. **Copper** is located below **Hydrogen**, while **Silver** and **Gold** are near the very bottom, indicating they are highly unreactive.
 
• A metal placed higher in the series can **displace** a metal placed lower in the series from its salt solution. This is known as a **displacement reaction**. Because **Sodium** is high in the series, it can displace almost any other metal listed below it.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Reactivity Series Hierarchy:**
 
 
• The typical order of metals from highest to lowest reactivity is: **Potassium (K)** > **Sodium (Na)** > **Calcium (Ca)** > **Magnesium (Mg)** > **Aluminium (Al)** > **Zinc (Zn)** > **Iron (Fe)** > **Lead (Pb)** > **Hydrogen (H)** > **Copper (Cu)** > **Mercury (Hg)** > **Silver (Ag)** > **Gold (Au)**.
 
• Metals above **Hydrogen** can displace it from acids to produce **hydrogen gas**, whereas metals like **Copper**, **Silver**, and **Gold** cannot.
 
 
 
• **Noble Metals (Gold and Silver):**
 
 
• **Gold** and **Silver** are often referred to as **noble metals** because they do not react with moisture, air, or ordinary acids. This property makes **Gold** (located at the very bottom) ideal for **jewelry** and **electronic components**.
 
• **Silver** is also highly unreactive but can tarnish over time when exposed to **sulfur** compounds in the air.
 
 
 
• **Transition Metal (Copper):**
 
 
• **Copper** is a **transition metal** used extensively in **electrical wiring** and **plumbing** due to its high conductivity and relatively low reactivity compared to alkali metals. It does not react with **water** or **dilute hydrochloric acid**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Storage of Sodium:** Because **Sodium** reacts explosively with **moisture** in the air, it must be stored under **kerosene** or **liquid paraffin** to prevent accidental combustion.
 
• **Extraction Methods:** The position in the reactivity series determines how a metal is extracted. Highly reactive metals like **Sodium** and **Potassium** are extracted via **electrolysis** of their molten chlorides, whereas less reactive metals like **Iron** are extracted by reduction with **carbon**.
 
• **Ionization Energy:** Reactivity is closely linked to **ionization energy**. Metals at the top, such as **Sodium**, have **low ionization energy**, meaning they lose their valence electrons very easily to form **positive ions (cations)**.
 
• **Reaction with Water:** While **Sodium** reacts violently with cold water, metals like **Magnesium** react only with **hot water**, and **Iron** reacts only with **steam**, further demonstrating the gradient of the **reactivity series**.
</ul

• In a large hall, sound needs to reach the audience sitting at the back just as clearly as those at the front. A **flat ceiling** might reflect sound in a way that creates "dead spots" or **sound shadows** where the audio is faint.
 
• By using a **curved surface** (acting similarly to a **concave mirror**), the reflected **sound waves** are distributed more **uniformly**. This ensures that the sound is **audible** and **intelligible** to every person in the **audience**.
 
• Because the purpose of the **curved design** (the assertion) is specifically to achieve this **even distribution** of sound (the reason), the reason provides the **correct logical explanation** for the assertion. ***Hence, both assertion and reason are true and the reason is the correct explanation.***

• **Multiple Reflections**: While **curved ceilings** help spread sound, **multiple reflections** can sometimes lead to **reverberation**. If the **time interval** between the original sound and reflected sound is too long, it can blur the **clarity** of speech.

• **Applications**: The principle of **curved reflection** is not limited to ceilings; it is also used in **stethoscopes**, **megaphones**, and **horns** to direct sound into a specific **direction** or **focal point**.

• **Auditory Uniformity**: The primary goal of **acoustic design** in **public buildings** is to achieve **uniformity** in **sound pressure levels** throughout the seating area.
 
• **Historical Context**: Even in **ancient Greek theaters**, the semi-circular **architectural design** was intended to amplify and project the **voice** of actors to the top rows of the **amphitheater**.

__
 
• **Catenation** is the unique property of **carbon** that allows it to form **covalent bonds** with other carbon atoms, leading to the formation of long, stable chains and structures.
 
• This property results in the creation of **straight chains**, **branched chains**, and **cyclic rings** of various sizes. The **Carbon-Carbon (C-C)** bond is extremely strong and stable, which is a major reason why carbon can form such a vast number of compounds.
 
• The small size of the **carbon atom** (atomic number **6**) enables its nucleus to hold the shared pairs of electrons strongly, ensuring the stability of these long chains. ***Hence, the correct answer is Catenation.***
 
• While other elements like **Silicon** also exhibit catenation, they can typically only form chains of up to **7 or 8 atoms**. These chains are highly reactive and unstable compared to the carbon chains found in organic chemistry.
 
• The sheer variety of carbon compounds, numbering in the **millions**, is primarily attributed to the combined effects of **catenation** and **tetravalency**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tetravalency of Carbon:**
 
 
• Carbon has **4 valence electrons** in its outermost shell. This means it can form **four covalent bonds** with other atoms of carbon or atoms of other monovalent elements like **Hydrogen**, **Oxygen**, **Nitrogen**, and **Sulphur**.
 
• This tetravalent nature allows carbon to create a diverse range of **functional groups**, which determine the chemical properties of the resulting organic molecules.
 
 
 
• **Isomerism:**
 
 
• **Isomerism** is a phenomenon where two or more compounds have the **same molecular formula** but **different structural arrangements** or spatial orientations.
 
• For example, **Butane (C4H10)** has two isomers: **n-butane** (straight chain) and **isobutane** (branched chain). This adds to the massive variety of carbon-based substances.
 
 
 
• **Combustion:**
 
 
• **Combustion** is a chemical process where a substance reacts rapidly with **Oxygen** and gives off heat. Carbon and its compounds are used as excellent fuels because they release a large amount of energy during combustion, typically producing **CO2** and **H2O**.
 
 
 
• **Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds:**
 
 
• Carbon atoms can be linked by **single**, **double**, or **triple bonds**. Compounds with only single bonds are called **Saturated** (e.g., **Alkanes**), while those with double or triple bonds are called **Unsaturated** (e.g., **Alkenes** and **Alkynes**).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Organic Chemistry:** Due to catenation, a separate branch of chemistry called **Organic Chemistry** was developed to study carbon-containing compounds.
 
• **Allotropes of Carbon:** Carbon exists in different physical forms in the same state, known as allotropes. The most famous include **Diamond** (3D network), **Graphite** (layers), and **Buckminsterfullerene (C60)** (spherical).
 
• **Bond Energy:** The bond energy of a **C-C bond** is approximately **348 kJ/mol**, which is significantly higher than **Si-Si bonds** (around **222 kJ/mol**), explaining why carbon chains are more durable.
</ul

questions.question: Which process best explains how water droplets form on the outer surface of a cold glass during a hot day?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Condensation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Condensation** is the physical process by which **water vapor** (gas) in the air is converted into **liquid water**. This occurs when the air temperature drops to its **dew point**.
 
• On a hot day, the air surrounding a cold glass contains **invisible water vapor**. When this warm, moist air comes into contact with the **cold exterior surface** of the glass, the air's temperature rapidly decreases.
 
• As the temperature of the air near the glass falls, the **water molecules** lose **kinetic energy** and move more slowly. This reduction in energy causes the molecules to **cluster together**, transitioning from a gaseous state to form **liquid droplets**.
 
• The appearance of these droplets is a direct result of the air reaching **saturation** at the colder temperature provided by the glass. Since cold air cannot hold as much moisture as warm air, the **excess water vapor** must transition into liquid form.
 
• This process is the exact **opposite of evaporation**, where liquid water gains energy to become a gas. ***Hence, the correct answer is Condensation.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Evaporation:**
 
 
• This is the process by which **liquid water** turns into **water vapor** or gas. It occurs when water molecules at the surface gain enough **thermal energy** to break free from the attractive forces of other liquid molecules.
 
• It is a **cooling process** because the higher-energy molecules leave the liquid, reducing the average temperature of the remaining substance. Common examples include **sweat evaporating** from skin or water drying from **wet clothes**.
 
 
 
• **Freezing:**
 
 
• Freezing is the phase transition in which a **liquid** turns into a **solid**. For pure water at standard atmospheric pressure, this occurs at **0 degrees Celsius** (**32 degrees Fahrenheit**).
 
• During this process, **heat energy** is released into the environment as the molecules lose energy and form a **fixed crystalline structure** (ice).
 
 
 
• **Sublimation:**
 
 
• This is a relatively rare phase change where a **solid** transforms directly into a **gas** without passing through the intermediate **liquid state**.
 
• A well-known example is **dry ice** (solid carbon dioxide), which "smokes" as it turns into gas at **room temperature**. In nature, this can happen to **snow or ice** in extremely cold, dry, and windy conditions.
 
 
 
• **Deposition:**
 
 
• Deposition is the reverse of sublimation, where **water vapor** changes directly into **solid ice**.
 
• This is responsible for the formation of **frost** on grass or windowpanes during cold **winter nights** when the surface temperature is below the **freezing point**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Humidity and Dew Point:**
 
 
• **Relative Humidity** is the ratio of the current **water vapor pressure** to the **saturation vapor pressure** at a given temperature. When it reaches **100%**, the air is saturated.
 
• The **Dew Point** is the specific **temperature** to which air must be cooled to become saturated with water vapor. If the glass surface is below this temperature, **condensation** will inevitably occur.
 
 
 
• **Latent Heat:**
 
 
• During **condensation**, energy known as **latent heat of condensation** is released. This release of energy is a major driver of **atmospheric phenomena**, such as the development of **thunderstorms** and **hurricanes**.
 
• In the case of the cold glass, the **thermal energy** from the water vapor is transferred to the **glass and the liquid inside**, which is why a cold drink warms up faster in **humid environments**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Two planets have the same radius. Planet A has twice the mass of Planet B. What is the ratio of acceleration due to gravity on Planet A to that on Planet B?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2 : 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **acceleration due to gravity (g)** on the surface of a planet is the acceleration experienced by an object due to the **gravitational force** exerted by that planet.
 
• The mathematical formula to calculate this is **g = (G * M) / R²**, where **G** is the **Universal Gravitational Constant**, **M** is the **mass of the planet**, and **R** is the **radius of the planet**.
 
• In the given problem, it is stated that **Planet A** and **Planet B** have the **same radius** (R_A = R_B). Since the radius is constant, the acceleration due to gravity is **directly proportional to the mass** of the planet (g ∝ M).
 
• The question mentions that **Planet A has twice the mass of Planet B** (M_A = 2 * M_B). This means that if we substitute these values into the ratio, we get **g_A / g_B = (M_A / M_B) * (R_B² / R_A²)**.
 
• Because the radii are equal, the term (R_B² / R_A²) becomes **1**. Therefore, the ratio of their accelerations due to gravity is equal to the ratio of their masses, which is **2 : 1**. ***Hence, the ratio g_A : g_B is 2 : 1.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Universal Gravitational Constant (G):**
 
 
• This is a physical constant involved in the calculation of gravitational effects. Its value is approximately **6.674 x 10^-11 Nm²/kg²**.
 
• It was first measured by **Henry Cavendish** in the year **1798** using a torsion balance.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting 'g':**
 
 
• **Mass**: If the mass of a planet increases while the radius remains the same, the **gravitational pull increases** linearly.
 
• **Radius**: If the radius of a planet increases while the mass remains the same, the **acceleration due to gravity decreases** according to the **inverse square law**.
 
 
 
• **Acceleration due to gravity on Earth:**
 
 
• The standard value of **g** on the surface of **Earth** is **9.8 m/s²** (or roughly 32.2 ft/s²).
 
• This value is not uniform across the globe; it is slightly **higher at the poles** and **lower at the equator** due to the Earth's **oblate spheroid** shape and its rotation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Independence of Object Mass:** The **acceleration due to gravity** is independent of the mass of the object that is falling. Whether it is a heavy rock or a light feather (in a vacuum), both will fall with the **same acceleration** on the same planet.
 
• **Variation with Altitude and Depth:**
 
 
• The value of **g decreases with altitude** as you move away from the center of the planet.
 
• The value of **g also decreases with depth** as you move toward the center of the planet, eventually becoming **zero at the center**.
 
 
 
• **Weight vs. Mass:** While **mass** is an intrinsic property of matter and remains **constant** everywhere, **weight (W = m * g)** is a force that changes depending on the **acceleration due to gravity** of the location.

__
 
• **Fertilisation** in flowering plants is the process where **male gametes** (carried by pollen) fuse with the **female gamete** (egg) inside the **ovule** to form a **zygote**.
 
• Once fertilisation is complete, the floral parts undergo significant transformations to protect the developing embryo and facilitate the next generation.

• The **petals, sepals, stamens, style, and stigma** usually wither and fall off after fertilisation because their roles in attracting pollinators and receiving pollen are no longer required. ***Hence, statements 2 and 4 are incorrect.***

• **Zygote to Embryo:** Following fertilisation, the **zygote** undergoes multiple cell divisions to become the **embryo**, which is the "baby plant" housed within the **seed**.
 
• **Seed Structure:** A mature seed consists of a **seed coat**, **cotyledons** (seed leaves), and an **embryo axis** (consisting of the **radicle** and **plumule**).

• **Hormonal Control:** The transformation of the ovary into a fruit is largely regulated by plant hormones such as **auxins**, **gibberellins**, and **ethylene**.
 
• **Persistent Sepals:** In some species, the **sepals** do not fall off but remain attached to the fruit, such as in **brinjal (eggplant)**, **chilli**, and **strawberry**.
 
• **Seed Germination:** The **seed** remains in a state of **dormancy** until it finds favorable conditions (water, air, and suitable temperature) to grow into a **seedling**.

questions.question: A car's velocity-time graph is a straight line parallel to the x-axis at 40 km/h. What will the area enclosed between the graph and the time axis from t = 0 to t = 3 hours represent?

options.text: Displacement of the car in 3 hours

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Displacement of the car in 3 hours**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The area under a **velocity-time graph** (v-t graph) represents the **displacement** of the object during that specific **time interval**.
 
• In this scenario, the graph is a **straight line parallel** to the **time axis** (x-axis), which indicates that the car is moving with a **uniform velocity** of **40 km/h**.
 
• The area enclosed between the graph and the time axis forms a **rectangle**. The height of this rectangle corresponds to the **velocity** (40 km/h) and the width corresponds to the **time duration** (3 hours).
 
• By calculating the area (**Length x Breadth**), we get **40 km/h multiplied by 3 hours**, which equals **120 km**. This numerical value represents the total **displacement** covered by the car in **3 hours**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• Since the velocity is **constant** and the graph is **horizontal**, the **slope** of the line is **zero**. This means the **acceleration** of the car is **zero**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **final velocity** is simply the value on the y-axis (40 km/h) and is not represented by the **area** under the curve. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• While the numerical value of **average speed** would be 40 km/h in this specific case of uniform motion in a straight line, the **area** specifically denotes the **physical quantity** of **displacement** (or distance), not the **rate** itself. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Displacement:** It is defined as the **shortest distance** between the **initial** and **final positions** of an object. It is a **vector quantity**, meaning it has both **magnitude** and **direction**. The **SI unit** of displacement is the **meter (m)**.
 
• **Velocity-Time Graph Characteristics:**
 
 
• A **straight line** with a **positive slope** indicates **uniform acceleration**.
 
• A **straight line** with a **negative slope** indicates **uniform retardation** (deceleration).
 
• A **curved line** indicates **non-uniform acceleration**.
 
• The **slope** of the v-t graph at any point gives the **instantaneous acceleration**.
 
 
 
• **Uniform Motion:** When an object covers **equal distances** in **equal intervals of time**, it is said to be in **uniform motion**. In this state, the **velocity remains constant** throughout the journey, as seen in this **40 km/h** example.
 
• **Relationship Equation:** The fundamental relationship for **constant velocity** is **Displacement = Velocity x Time**. Geometrically, this is exactly what the **area of the rectangle** under the v-t graph calculates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Area vs. Slope:** It is vital to distinguish that the **area** under a velocity-time graph gives **displacement**, whereas the **slope** of the same graph gives **acceleration**.
 
• **Distance vs. Displacement:** If the velocity-time graph stays above the **time axis** (positive velocity), the **area** represents both **distance** and **magnitude of displacement**. However, if the graph goes below the axis, the area above is positive and the area below is negative for calculating **displacement**, while both are added as positive values for **total distance**.
 
• **Units:** Always ensure the **units** are consistent. In this problem, **km/h** and **hours** are used, resulting in **km**. If the time were in minutes, it would need to be converted to **hours** or the velocity converted to **km/min** before calculating the **area**.
</ul

questions.question: When a person touches a hot object, there is a delay in the muscle response. Which part of the nervous tissue is directly responsible for carrying the nerve impulse to the muscle to bring about a quick movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Axon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Axon** is a long, slender projection of a **Neuron** (nerve cell) that typically conducts electrical impulses, known as **Action Potentials**, away from the nerve cell body or **Soma**. In the context of a quick muscle response, it is the **Axon** of a **Motor Neuron** that carries the signal directly to the muscle fibers. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Dendrites** are the branch-like structures of a neuron that are designed to **receive communications** from other cells. They conduct electrical messages to the neuron cell body for the cell to function; they do not carry the impulse away to the muscle. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Nucleus** is located within the cell body (**Soma**) of the neuron. It contains the **Genetic Material** (DNA) and coordinates the cell's activities like growth and reproduction, but it is not involved in the actual transmission of the **Nerve Impulse** along the length of the cell to an effector. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Connective tissue** in the nervous system, such as the **Epineurium**, **Perineurium**, and **Endoneurium**, provides structural support and protection to the bundles of axons (nerves). However, it is not a part of the nervous tissue that transmits electrical impulses. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• The specific pathway for a quick movement in response to a stimulus like heat is called a **Reflex Arc**, which bypasses the conscious brain to allow for an immediate reaction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of a Neuron:**
 
 
• A typical neuron consists of three main parts: the **Cell Body** (Soma), **Dendrites**, and an **Axon**.
 
• The **Myelin Sheath** is a fatty layer that surrounds the **Axon** of many neurons. Its primary function is to **increase the speed** at which electrical impulses propagate along the myelinated fiber.
 
• The gaps in the myelin sheath are known as **Nodes of Ranvier**, which facilitate the rapid "jumping" of the impulse (**Saltatory Conduction**).
 
 
 
• **The Reflex Arc Process:**
 
 
• When a hot object is touched, **Thermoreceptors** in the skin detect the stimulus.
 
• The **Sensory Neuron** carries the impulse to the **Spinal Cord**.
 
• A **Relay Neuron** (Interneuron) in the spinal cord transmits the signal to a **Motor Neuron**.
 
• The **Motor Neuron** then sends the impulse via its **Axon** to the **Effector** (the muscle), causing it to contract and pull the hand away.
 
 
 
• **Synapse and Neurotransmitters:**
 
 
• The **Synapse** is the small gap between the **Axon Terminal** of one neuron and the **Dendrite** of the next.
 
• Communication across this gap occurs via chemical messengers called **Neurotransmitters**, such as **Acetylcholine**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Neuromuscular Junction:** This is the specific chemical synapse formed by the contact between a **Motor Neuron** and a **Muscle Fiber**. It is at this junction that the **Axon** transmits the signal that triggers muscle contraction.
 
• **Direction of Impulse:** In a neuron, the nerve impulse always travels in one direction: from the **Dendrites** to the **Cell Body**, and then along the **Axon** to the **Axon Terminals**.
 
• **Response Time:** While there is a slight delay due to synaptic transmission (the time it takes for neurotransmitters to cross the gap), the **Axon** is the structure that ensures the message travels over long distances (e.g., from the spine to the hand) at speeds up to **120 meters per second**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following statements about work is FALSE?

options.text: Work can be positive, negative, or zero.
Work is a path-independent quantity for all forces.
Work has the same units as energy.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Work is a path-independent quantity for all forces**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Conservative and Non-conservative Forces**: Work done by a force is **path-independent** only if the force is a **conservative force** (such as **gravity**, **electrostatic force**, or **spring force**). For **non-conservative forces** like **friction** or **air resistance**, the work done depends entirely on the **actual path** taken between two points. Therefore, work is not path-independent for **all forces**. ***Hence, statement 2 is false.***
 
• **Nature of Work**: Work is defined as the **dot product** of the **force vector** and the **displacement vector**. It can be **positive** (when the angle between force and displacement is **less than 90 degrees**), **negative** (when the angle is **greater than 90 degrees**), or **zero** (when force is **perpendicular** to displacement or displacement is zero). ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Units and Dimensions**: Work is a **scalar quantity** and has the same **SI unit** as energy, which is the **Joule (J)**. In **CGS units**, it is measured in **Ergs**. Both work and energy share the same dimensional formula: **[M1 L2 T-2]**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Energy Transfer**: Work is often described as **energy in transit**. It is a mechanism through which **energy is transferred** from one system to another or converted from one form to another through the application of force over a distance. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Work is a path-independent quantity for all forces.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Work-Energy Theorem**: This theorem states that the **net work done** by all forces acting on a body is equal to the **change in its kinetic energy**. This relationship highlights that work and energy are fundamentally linked.
 
• **Conservative Forces Details**: A force is conservative if the **work done** by it in moving a particle around any **closed loop** is **zero**. Examples include **magnetic force** and **central forces**. The work done by these forces depends only on the **initial and final positions**.
 
• **Non-conservative Forces Details**: These forces cause **dissipation of energy**, usually in the form of **heat** or **sound**. Because the work done against **friction** increases with the **length of the path**, it cannot be recovered as potential energy.
 
• **Zero Work Examples**: A common example of **zero work** is a person carrying a heavy load on their head while walking horizontally; here, the **gravitational force** is **perpendicular (90 degrees)** to the direction of motion. Another example is **centripetal force** in circular motion.
 
• **Conversion Factor**: It is important to note the relationship between different units of work: **1 Joule** is equal to **10⁷ Ergs**. One Joule is defined as the work done by a force of **1 Newton** causing a displacement of **1 meter**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mathematical Expression**: The formula for work is **W = Fs cos(theta)**, where **F** is the magnitude of force, **s** is displacement, and **theta** is the angle between them.
 
• **Power Correlation**: The **rate** at which work is done is known as **Power**. It is measured in **Watts (W)**, where **1 Watt = 1 Joule per second**.
 
• **Sign Convention**: **Positive work** increases the energy of the system (e.g., accelerating an object), while **negative work** decreases the energy of the system (e.g., a car braking due to friction).
</ul

questions.question: A ray passing through which of the following parts of a lens emerges undeviated?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Optical centre**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **optical centre** of a lens is a specific point located on the **principal axis** such that any ray of light passing through it emerges without any **deviation**.
 
• In the case of a **thin lens**, the optical centre is considered the **geometric centre** of the lens. Light rays incident at this point pass straight through because the two **refracting surfaces** are effectively **parallel** at the center, leading to zero **lateral displacement**.
 
• This property is fundamental in **ray optics** and is used to simplify **ray diagrams** for both **convex** and **concave** lenses.
 
• While light rays passing through other parts of the lens (like the focus or between the focus and center) undergo **refraction** and change their direction, the ray through the **optical centre** maintains its original path. ***Hence, the correct answer is Optical centre.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Principal Focus (F):**
 
 
• For a **convex lens**, it is the point where rays **parallel** to the principal axis **converge** after refraction.
 
• For a **concave lens**, it is the point from which rays parallel to the principal axis appear to **diverge**.
 
• A ray passing through the **Principal Focus** will emerge **parallel** to the principal axis after passing through the lens. Thus, it **deviates** from its original path.
 
 
 
• **Centre of Curvature (C):**
 
 
• A lens has two spherical surfaces, and the center of these spheres are called the **centres of curvature** (C1 and C2).
 
• The distance from the **optical centre** to the **centre of curvature** is the **radius of curvature (R)**.
 
• Unlike mirrors, a ray passing through the centre of curvature of a lens **does undergo refraction** and deviation unless it specifically coincides with the optical center.
 
 
 
• **Principal Axis:**
 
 
• It is the **imaginary straight line** passing through the two **centres of curvature** and the **optical centre** of the lens.
 
• It serves as the **reference line** for measuring all distances, such as **object distance (u)**, **image distance (v)**, and **focal length (f)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lens Maker's Formula:** The relationship between **focal length**, **refractive index**, and **radii of curvature** is given by **1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)**.
 
• **Thin Lens Approximation:** In most **general physics** problems, we assume lenses are **thin**. In thick lenses, the ray passing through the **optical centre** might experience a tiny **lateral shift**, though its **angular deviation** remains zero.
 
• **Sign Convention:** According to the **Cartesian sign convention**, the **optical centre (O)** is taken as the **origin**. Distances measured in the direction of **incident light** are positive, while those opposite are negative.
 
• **Aperture:** The **effective diameter** of the circular outline of a spherical lens is called its **aperture**, which determines the **intensity** of light entering the lens.
</ul

The HCF of given numbers always divides the difference between any pair of those numbers.

Difference between 172 and 148 = 24

questions.question: The cost of 2 balls and 3 bats is ₹ 84. The cost of 3 balls and 1 bat is ₹ 63. What is the cost of 5 balls and 3 bats ?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let the cost of 1 ball be x and 1 bat be y. We have:

2x + 3y = 84 ... (i)

3x + y = 63 ⇒ 9x + 3y = 189 ... (ii)

Subtracting (i) from (ii) gives: 7x = 105 ⇒ x = 15

Required cost = 5x + 3y = (2x + 3y) + 3x = 84 + 3 × 15 = 84 + 45 = 129

**∴ The correct answer is ₹ 129.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Cost of 2 balls and 3 bats = ₹ 84

Cost of 3 balls and 1 bat = ₹ 63

**Calculation:**

Let the cost of 1 ball be x and the cost of 1 bat be y.

⇒ 2x + 3y = 84 ... (1)

⇒ 3x + y = 63 ... (2)

From equation (2), expressing y in terms of x:

⇒ y = 63 − 3x

Substituting the value of y into equation (1):

⇒ 2x + 3(63 − 3x) = 84

⇒ 2x + 189 − 9x = 84

⇒ 189 − 7x = 84

⇒ 7x = 189 − 84

⇒ 7x = 105

⇒ x = 15

Now, substituting x = 15 into equation (2):

⇒ y = 63 − 3 × 15

⇒ y = 63 − 45 = 18

We need to find the cost of 5 balls and 3 bats:

⇒ Cost = 5x + 3y

⇒ Cost = 5 × 15 + 3 × 18

⇒ Cost = 75 + 54 = 129

**∴ The correct answer is ₹ 129.**

questions.question: In October 2025, which of the following regulatory authorities restricted the commercial use of the term 'ORS' in beverages?

options.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Food Safety and Standards Authority of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)** issued a strict directive in **October 2025** to restrict the commercial use of the term **'ORS'** (Oral Rehydration Salts) by food business operators for beverages that do not meet medical standards.
 
• The regulatory body observed that many companies were marketing sugary drinks and fruit juices under the name **'ORS'**, which could mislead consumers into believing these products are medicinal rehydration solutions. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• According to the **FSSAI**, the term **'ORS'** is a scientific terminology used specifically for a composition defined by the **World Health Organization (WHO)** or the **Indian Pharmacopoeia** for treating clinical dehydration.
 
• The authority mandated that only those products manufactured under a **drug license** and meeting the specific electrolyte composition can use the abbreviation **'ORS'**.
 
• Any beverage that does not comply with these standards must be labeled as an **'Electrolyte Drink'** or a **'Rehydration Beverage'**, and must carry a disclaimer that the product is not a medical **ORS**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI):**
 
 
• It was established under the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006**, which consolidated various older laws related to food safety in India.
 
• The organization operates under the administrative control of the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**, Government of India.
 
• Headquartered in **New Delhi**, its primary function is to lay down science-based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale, and import.
 
 
 
• **Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS):**
 
 
• **ORS** is a mixture of **Sodium Chloride (2.6g)**, **Glucose (13.5g)**, **Potassium Chloride (1.5g)**, and **Trisodium Citrate (2.9g)** when dissolved in **1 litre** of water.
 
• It is used as a life-saving treatment for dehydration caused by **diarrhea** or **cholera**, specifically by replacing lost fluids and essential salts.
 
• Using fruit beverages labeled as **'ORS'** during medical emergencies can be dangerous as they often contain **high sugar levels**, which may worsen certain types of diarrhea.
 
 
 
• **Other Regulatory Bodies:**
 
 
• **Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS):** It provides technical knowledge on medical and public health matters but does not directly regulate food labeling.
 
• **Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR):** It is the apex body in India for the formulation, coordination, and promotion of **biomedical research**.
 
• **National Medical Commission (NMC):** This body regulates medical education and professionals in India, replacing the former Medical Council of India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mislabeling and Penalties:** Under the **FSS Act**, misbranding or providing misleading information on food labels can attract heavy penalties and lead to the suspension of the **FSSAI license**.
 
• **Consumer Awareness:** The **2025** directive aims to protect vulnerable populations, especially children, by ensuring that parents do not confuse commercial sugary drinks with clinical **rehydration therapy**.
 
• **WHO Guidelines:** The **WHO** first recommended a standard **ORS** formula in **1975**, and the osmolarity was further reduced in **2002** to improve efficacy.
</ul

questions.question: In the Union Budget, 2025–26, the Government of India announced a comprehensive multi-sectoral 'Rural Prosperity and Resilience' programme that aims ______________.

options.text: to address the drop out problem in school
to develop the sports facilities in rural areas
to address administrative problems in rural areas

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**to address under-employment in agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Union Budget 2025–26**, presented by the Union Finance Minister **Nirmala Sitharaman** on **February 1, 2025**, introduced the **'Rural Prosperity and Resilience'** programme as a cornerstone for rural development.
 
• The primary objective of this programme is **to address under-employment in agriculture** by facilitating the transition of the rural workforce into more productive and diverse economic activities. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• It emphasizes **multi-sectoral interventions**, focusing on **diversifying** the rural economy beyond traditional crop cultivation into areas like **food processing**, **animal husbandry**, and **rural entrepreneurship**.
 
• The programme aims to build **resilience** against economic and climate-related shocks by promoting **climate-resilient agriculture** and enhancing the **income-generating capacity** of rural households.
 
• By addressing **disguised unemployment** (a form of under-employment prevalent in Indian farming), the government intends to optimize **labour productivity** and ensure **sustainable livelihoods** for the rural population.
 
• The initiative does not primarily focus on school dropout rates, sports infrastructure, or administrative reforms, though these may be addressed by other specific schemes like **Samagra Shiksha** or **Khelo India**. ***Hence, statements 1, 3, and 4 are incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Budget 2025-26 Themes:**
 
 
• The budget focuses on four major pillars: **Garib** (Poor), **Mahila** (Women), **Yuva** (Youth), and **Annadata** (Farmers), often referred to as the **GYAN** initiative.
 
• The **'Rural Prosperity and Resilience'** programme aligns with the **Annadata** pillar to boost **farm incomes** and modernize the **agrarian economy**.
 
 
 
• **Under-employment in India:**
 
 
• **Under-employment**, particularly **disguised unemployment**, occurs when more people are engaged in an activity than are actually required. In **India**, nearly **45-47%** of the workforce is dependent on **agriculture**, which contributes only about **15-18%** to the **GDP**.
 
• The **Rural Prosperity** scheme seeks to bridge this gap by creating **non-farm jobs** in rural areas, such as in **logistics**, **warehousing**, and **agri-tech startups**.
 
 
 
• **Components of Rural Resilience:**
 
 
• **Resilience** involves the capacity of rural communities to withstand **climate change** impacts. The budget allocates funds for **micro-irrigation**, **digital public infrastructure** for agriculture, and **natural farming**.
 
• The **National Cooperative Policy** is also integrated to empower **Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)** for better credit flow to small farmers.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Impact:** By targeting **under-employment**, the government aims to increase the **disposable income** of rural families, which in turn boosts **domestic consumption** and fuels national **economic growth**.
 
• **Focus on Women:** A significant portion of the programme is expected to support **Lakhpati Didis** (women in Self-Help Groups) to engage in **value-addition** and **small-scale industries** within the **rural sector**.
 
• **Date of Announcement:** The scheme was officially proposed during the budget speech on **1st February 2025**, marking a shift toward **long-term structural reforms** in the **rural landscape**.
 
• **Multi-sectoral Approach:** It integrates **infrastructure development** (roads and storage) with **skill development** to ensure that the rural population is equipped for **new-age employment** opportunities.

questions.question: What was India’s overall score in the Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) for the year 2024 released in February 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**38**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI)** for the year **2024** was released in **February 2025** by the international non-governmental organization **Transparency International**.
 
• In this latest report, **India** recorded an overall score of **38** out of **100**. This score represents the perceived level of public sector corruption in the country based on expert assessments and surveys.
 
• The **CPI** uses a scale of **0 to 100**, where **0** signifies that a country is "highly corrupt" and **100** signifies that a country is "very clean." A score of **38** indicates that India continues to face significant challenges in institutional transparency and anti-corruption measures.
 
• Comparing the current data with previous years, India’s score has seen a slight decline from the **2023** score, which was **39**. In **2022**, the score was **40**, indicating a downward trend in perceived integrity over the last few cycles.
 
• The **2024** index evaluated a total of **180 countries** and territories, providing a comprehensive global overview of corruption levels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Transparency International:**
 
 
• It is a global movement working in over **100 countries** to end the injustice of corruption.
 
• The organization was founded in **May 1993** and is headquartered in **Berlin, Germany**.
 
• Its primary mission is to promote **transparency, accountability, and integrity** at all levels and in all sectors of society.
 
 
 
• **Methodology of CPI:**
 
 
• The **CPI** aggregates data from **13 different data sources** from **12 independent institutions**.
 
• These institutions include the **World Bank**, the **World Economic Forum**, and private risk and consulting companies.
 
• The index specifically focuses on **public sector corruption**, including bribery, diversion of public funds, and the ability of governments to contain corruption.
 
 
 
• **Global Performance Trends:**
 
 
• Consistently top-performing countries usually include **Denmark**, **Finland**, and **New Zealand**, often scoring above **85**.
 
• Countries at the bottom of the index typically include **Somalia**, **South Sudan**, and **Syria**, often scoring below **15** due to prolonged conflict and weak governance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **India’s Regional Standing:**
 
 
• In the **South Asian** region, India’s performance is often compared with its neighbors. While it generally scores better than **Pakistan** and **Bangladesh**, it lags significantly behind **Bhutan**, which consistently maintains a high score and rank.
 
• The **2024** report highlighted that stagnation or decline in scores for many **G20** nations, including India, is a cause for concern regarding global economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Scores:**
 
 
• A low score in the **CPI** can negatively affect a country’s **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** as investors prefer environments with high legal certainty and low corruption.
 
• The report often accompanies recommendations for governments to strengthen **judicial independence** and protect **whistleblowers** to improve their standing in future indices.
 
• The **2024** index emphasized the link between **corruption** and **social inequality**, noting that corruption often disproportionately affects the most vulnerable populations.
 
 
</ul

• **Dadasaheb Phalke** directed India's first indigenous full-length feature film, **Raja Harishchandra**, in **1913**.

questions.question: Which city was reported among the top 10 most polluted cities in the world on December 28, 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Delhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Delhi**, the capital city of **India**, frequently appears in global rankings of the most polluted cities, especially during the **winter season**.
 
• On **December 28, 2025**, global air quality monitoring platforms like **IQAir** and the **World Air Quality Index** reported that **Delhi** was among the top 10 most polluted cities in the world based on real-time **PM2.5** concentrations.
 
• The **Air Quality Index (AQI)** in **Delhi** during late **December** often reaches the **"Severe"** or **"Hazardous"** category, frequently exceeding the **400** or **500** mark on the scale.
 
• While other Indian metropolitan cities like **Mumbai** and **Kolkata** have seen rising pollution levels, the geographical and climatic conditions of **Delhi** make its pollution significantly more persistent and dangerous during the **winter months**.
 
• The **Particulate Matter (PM2.5)** levels in **Delhi** during this period were recorded at levels many times higher than the safety limits prescribed by the **World Health Organization (WHO)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sources of Pollution in Delhi:**
 
 
• The primary contributors to **Delhi's** poor air quality include **vehicular emissions**, **industrial discharge**, and **construction dust** within the **National Capital Region (NCR)**.
 
• Seasonal factors such as **stubble burning** (parali) in neighboring states like **Punjab** and **Haryana** significantly spike pollution levels between **October** and **December**.
 
• In late **December**, the use of **biomass burning** for heating and **firecrackers** during various festivals also adds to the toxic load.
 
 
 
• **Meteorological Factors:**
 
 
• **Temperature Inversion**: During **winter**, a layer of warm air traps cooler air near the ground. This prevents pollutants from dispersing, creating a **smog** layer over the city.
 
• Low **wind speeds** and high **humidity** further prevent the dilution of particulate matter, keeping the **AQI** high for extended periods.
 
 
 
• **Impact of PM2.5:**
 
 
• **PM2.5** refers to atmospheric particulate matter that has a diameter of less than **2.5 micrometers**.
 
• Because of their small size, these particles can penetrate deep into the **lungs** and enter the **bloodstream**, causing **respiratory** and **cardiovascular** diseases.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP):** To combat severe pollution, the **Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)** implements **GRAP** in **Delhi-NCR**. This includes measures like banning **diesel generators**, stopping **construction activities**, and implementing the **odd-even** vehicle scheme when **AQI** crosses certain thresholds.
 
• **National Clean Air Programme (NCAP):** Launched in **2019**, this **Government of India** initiative aims for a **20% to 30%** reduction in **PM2.5** and **PM10** concentrations by **2024** (later extended to **2026**) across **131** non-attainment cities.
 
• **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB):** The **CPCB** is the statutory organization under the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change** that monitors air quality across **India** and provides the official **National Air Quality Index**.
 
• **WHO Air Quality Guidelines:** The **World Health Organization** tightened its guidelines in **2021**, stating that annual average concentrations of **PM2.5** should not exceed **5 µg/m³**. Most Indian cities, including **Delhi**, struggle to meet even the more relaxed national standards.

__
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, in **August 2025**, announced the appointment of **Indranil Bhattacharyya** as an **ex-officio member** of the **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**.
 
• **Indranil Bhattacharyya** currently serves as an **Executive Director** at the **Reserve Bank of India**.
 
• He was nominated by the **Central Board of the RBI** to replace **Rajiv Ranjan**, following the latter's transition or retirement from the role. ***Hence, the statement regarding the appointee is correct.***
 
• This appointment was strategically timed ahead of the **October policy meeting** to ensure the committee reached its full legislative strength of **six members** for interest rate deliberations.
 
• The **MPC** is the statutory body responsible for determining the **policy repo rate** required to achieve the inflation target while keeping the objective of **growth** in mind.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) Structure**:
 
 
• The committee consists of **six members**: three from the **RBI** (including the Governor) and three external members appointed by the **Central Government**.
 
• The **Governor of the RBI** acts as the **ex-officio Chairperson** of the committee.
 
• The **Deputy Governor** in charge of monetary policy also serves as an **ex-officio member**.
 
 
 
• **Legal Framework**:
 
 
• The **MPC** was constituted under Section **45ZB** of the amended **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**.
 
• The framework for the MPC was officially adopted in **2016** to bring more **transparency** and **accountability** to India's monetary policy decisions.
 
 
 
• **Inflation Targeting**:
 
 
• The **Government of India**, in consultation with the **RBI**, sets the inflation target once every **five years**.
 
• The current target is **4% Consumer Price Index (CPI)** inflation, with an upper tolerance limit of **6%** and a lower tolerance limit of **2%**.
 
 
 
• **Decision-making Process**:
 
 
• Each member of the **MPC** has **one vote**. In the event of a tie, the **RBI Governor** has a **casting vote**.
 
• The quorum for the meeting of the **MPC** is **four members**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Rajiv Ranjan**: He previously served as the **Executive Director** and was the **nominated ex-officio member** before **Indranil Bhattacharyya** took over the responsibility in **2024/2025**.
 
• **Meeting Frequency**: The **MPC** is required to meet at least **four times a year**, though it typically meets **bi-monthly** (six times a year) to review the **macroeconomic situation**.
 
• **External Members**: These members are typically experts in the field of **economics**, **banking**, or **finance** and hold office for a period of **four years**.
